newsitem.title: ICELAND: Icelandic volcano could cause flooding "in hours".
newsitem.headline: Icelandic volcano could cause flooding "in hours".

text.p: Violent volcanic eruptions beneath Iceland's Vatnajokull glacier showed no sign of abating on Saturday and scientists said mounting flood-waters could break through the ice in a matter of hours.

Most of the volcanic activity was still hidden by a 500 to 700 metre (1,600 to 2,300 ft) thick cap of ice, but a dense black column of ash towered 300 metres (1,000 feet) above the vast fissure opened up by the six-day eruption.
The water level in the nearby Grimsvoen lake under the glacier was reported to be still rising.
Scientists are predicting flooding from the glacier towards the south coast of the island within hours or days as the intense heat deep within the glacier melts the ice.

The inhospitable glacial region 190 km (120 miles) to the east of Reykjavik is uninhabited, but flooding could cause widespread damage to roads, bridges and power lines in the area, and local power stations are also at risk.
Geologists said there was also a risk of contamination from the ash, which contains poisonous flourides.
The financial cost to the tiny island economy, which supports a population of just 250,000, could be devastating.

The eruption, which began on Monday, smashed through the Vatnajokull glacier two days later, spewing black clouds into the air and forming an evil-smelling tower of ash which was visible from most parts of Iceland.
Occasional bursts of red lightning lit up the air over the 10-km long fissure.
The eruption itself was accompanied by volcanic tremors, some registering over four points on the open-ended Richter scale, but these had subsided, experts said.
Air traffic controllers said many airlines had requested permission to fly over the eruption to give passengers a view of the eruption.

Scientists said one positive aspect of the eruption was that cod stocks off the south coast would benefit from the huge influx of fresh water into the sea as flooded rivers from the glacier reached the ocean.
